props.title: Paranormal Activity
props.initialSlug: Found footage horror exposes a couple's haunting

sections.content: Paranormal Activity (2007) revolutionized found-footage horror by stripping supernatural terror down to its bare essentials. Shot for just $15,000, Oren Peli's debut proved that a stationary camera, subtle sound design, and mounting dread could terrify audiences more effectively than gore or jump scares. The film follows the same innovative path blazed by The Blair Witch Project (1999), but trades woods for suburbia, creating an intimate haunted house story that feels unnervingly real. Its success spawned numerous imitators and five direct sequels, though none matched the original's raw intensity.

sections.content: The found footage subgenre experienced a massive resurgence following Paranormal Activity's success. Films like Cloverfield (2008) applied the technique to monster movies, while V/H/S (2012) created an anthology format allowing multiple directors to experiment with the style. Host (2020) modernized the approach by setting its supernatural horror entirely within a Zoom call during lockdown, proving the format continues to evolve with technology.

What sets Paranormal Activity apart is its masterful build of tension through mundane moments. Like The Haunting (1963), it understands that suggesting horror is more effective than showing it. The film's innovative use of security camera footage creates a sense of helpless observation as the supernatural presence grows bolder. This influenced later works like Unfriended (2014) and Searching (2018), which tell stories entirely through screens and surveillance. SUBHEAD: The Impact on Modern Horror

movies.title: Grave Encounters
movies.slug: A ghost hunting reality TV crew locks themselves in an abandoned psychiatric hospital for a night of filming. Their footage reveals real supernatural horror.

sections.content: Paranormal Activity's massive box office success ($193 million worldwide from a $15,000 budget) transformed low-budget horror filmmaking. Studios like Blumhouse Productions built their business model around micro-budget horror films that could potentially explode into profitable franchises. Films like Insidious (2010) and Sinister (2012) followed this template, while maintaining Paranormal Activity's focus on building atmospheric dread rather than relying on expensive special effects.
